Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines · Body, health & movement

tired adjective

also tiredness, I’m so tired, fatigued, worn out, exhausted, weary

classical

Cic. Ac. 1.1: dē viā fessus (Lewis & Short)
Sall. Jug. 53.5 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 313
Traupman 35, 39, 395

fessus, fessa, fessum

declension

tired, weary, worn out

The standard classical word, in prose and in verse (Lewis & Short: classical, especially frequent in the poets).

Other words

  • lassus, lassa, lassum — tired, weary, worn out

    declension · classical · Plaut. Amph. 329: Lassus sum hercle, nāvī ut vectus hūc sum; Plaut. Asin. 873

    (vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī et poētārum: Plaut., Hor., Juv.; nōn apud Cic. aut Caes.)

    The everyday word of comedy and of the poets, the source of Italian lasso and French las. Lewis & Short notes that it is not in Cicero or Caesar, who say fessus and dēfessus. Plautus and Terence, for their part, say lassus (twelve times) and dēfessus (thirteen) and happen not to have fessus: that shows the register of comedy, not that fessus is rare or wrong.

  • fatīgātus, fatīgāta, fatīgātum — worn out, exhausted

    adjective (participle of fatīgō), declension · also used · classical · Lewis & Short, s.v. fatīgō; Andresian p. 36

    Wearied by something; stronger than fessus, and rare before Augustus (Lewis & Short).

  • dēfessus, dēfessa, dēfessum — tired out, worn out

    adjective (participle of dēfetīscor), often with the ablative of a gerund: dēfessus ambulandō, declension · also used · classical · Ter. Ad. 713: Dēfessus sum ambulandō.; Plaut. Stich. 313: dēfessus sum pultandō

    The word of the comedies and of Cicero for being tired out by doing something. Classical and frequent as a participle (Lewis & Short s.v. dēfetīscor).

Examples

  • Fessus es?

    Are you tired? Said to a boy.composed

  • Fessa es?

    Are you tired? Said to a girl.composed

  • Tam fessa sum.

    I’m so tired.Traupman 35

  • Lassus sum hercle, nāvī ut vectus hūc sum: etiam nunc nauseō.

    I’m worn out, by Hercules, after coming here by ship: I still feel seasick.Plaut. Amph. 329

  • Dēfessus sum ambulandō.

    I’m worn out with walking.Ter. Ad. 713

  • ille opere forīs faciendō lassus noctū ad mē advenit

    he comes home to me at night tired from working out of doorsPlaut. Asin. 873

See also rest, run, pant, sleepy.
